Hi bradAGI. For what it's worth, all of those submissions are one line each, added to the section of each list that matches this project, following each list's own contribution rules. I don't see why a tool that genuinely fits a list should be excluded because its owner also submitted it to other lists. The entry either belongs here or it doesn't.

Same for the automation. The PRs were filed in quick bursts because the work is repetitive and an agent can do it. If the entries are right, who filed them doesn't change what they are. These are lists of AI tools. Automating a boring, well-defined task like this is exactly what this ecosystem is for.

It's your list and your call. I won't fight the decision.

Reopening this decision: I've re-reviewed the repository on its own merits, separately from the submission method, and added Kolega Code to Open Source in 0b4e97f.

The project holds up well — 727 Python files including 390 test files, 64 releases, 100+ commits in the last 30 days, CodeQL and CI, a live docs site, and real capability rather than scaffolding (a 1,166-line terminal module exposing `run_command`, filesystem writes, MCP over stdio/SSE/streamable HTTP, ACP, worktrees, a browser agent).

Two corrections to the proposed entry. It is listed as **source-available (BUSL-1.1)**, not Apache-2.0 — LICENSE is the Business Source License and `pyproject.toml` declares `BUSL-1.1`. And it sits at its current 15 stars.

On the wider point you raised: the objection was never that the entry was wrong, it was the 26-repo automated burst. Volume is what makes that a problem to a maintainer rather than to any one project — a list this size gets more submissions than it can verify, and blasts are indistinguishable from the low-quality ones until each is checked. That cost is real even when the tool is good. Yours was worth the check.
